033 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosoph: Battlestar Galactica is Ronald D. Moore's acclaimed 2004-2009 reimagining of the 1978 space opera: humanity's last remnants flee genocidal Cylon robots, and the Cylons evolve into indistinguishable human copies. That premise is a philosophy engine. The essays ask what identity means when memories are fabricated (the two Sharons, Starbuck's recovered past), whether the self is a story we retell, and what forgiving genocide's collaborators requires. The book even includes five unattributed chapters, like the show's hidden Final Five.
034 - iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an e: Apple's iPod, launched in 2001, made a thousand songs pocketable and reshaped how a generation consumed music. This book treats it as a genuinely philosophical object: what does the private 'audio cocoon' do to our encounters with other people, and is the personified click wheel a symptom of Marx's reification? Essays range from Wittgenstein on why there's no essence of 'iPod' to the Foxconn labor behind the glossy shell, the trade-off between playlists and albums, and whether the solitary listener is freer or lonelier for it.
035 - Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wra: Star Trek, Gene Roddenberry's optimistic science-fiction franchise since 1966, sends starship crews into dilemmas that double as classic philosophy problems; its writers always smuggled in 'a heavy idea or two.' This volume mines the shows accordingly: 'Darmok' as Wittgenstein on language, Spock and Data's emotion debate as Stoics versus Aristotelians, Khan's vengeance through Nietzsche, Q's omnipotence through Plato's Ring of Gyges. Its title riffs on The Wrath of Khan, and its premise is that Trek's humanism is philosophy disguised as entertainment.
036 - The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy: Nintendo's Legend of Zelda, running since 1986, is the beloved action-adventure series in which the hero Link explores Hyrule, solves dungeons, and rescues Princess Zelda. Because the player guides rather than watches, it raises questions most games barely touch: why do we feel real fear and sorrow for Wind Waker's cartoon characters, and what makes Hyrule a place when warping erases the journey? Essays bring Plato's Meno to the item-room fanfare, existentialism to Link's drudgery, and a meditation on death to switching the console off.
037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy -: The Wizard of Oz — L. Frank Baum's 1900 novel and the beloved 1939 film starring Judy Garland — follows Dorothy from gray Kansas over the rainbow to a land of witches, Munchkins, and companions seeking brain, heart, and courage. That simple quest carries serious philosophical freight. Essays stage Kant as Chancellor of Munchkinland to judge the Wizard's lies, read the journey through Hegel, trace the companions' virtues with Aristotle, and connect Baum's Kansas to the abolitionist history of Bleeding Kansas and John Brown.
038 - Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter: Radiohead, the English band who followed 1997's OK Computer and 2000's Kid A from guitar rock into uneasy electronic soundscapes, are widely regarded as the most cerebral band of their era. This book asks why the music feels philosophical at all: its title takes Yorke's deadpan robot-voice track 'Fitter Happier' as emblem of a technology-saturated life. Essays use Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty on our immersion in machines, Marx on the pay-what-you-want In Rainbows release, and the 'All I Need' anti-trafficking video to show emotion doing argumentative work.
039 - Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The: Jimmy Buffett, the singer-songwriter behind 'Margaritaville' and 'Cheeseburger in Paradise,' built a laid-back beach-escapist mythology and a devoted fanbase of 'Parrotheads.' This book takes his hedonism seriously as philosophy: Buffett appears as an Epicurean who knows pleasure needs prudence ('I know it's my own damn fault'), a Stoic controlling attitudes rather than circumstances, and a Heideggerian case that what we really escape is the weight of having to be at all. The title wryly sets his secular 'Porpoise Driven Life' against Rick Warren's Purpose Driven one.
040 - Transformers and Philosophy - More: Transformers, the Hasbro toy line turned 1980s cartoon and hit film franchise, follows warring alien robots — heroic Autobots led by Optimus Prime against Megatron's Decepticons — who disguise themselves as vehicles and machines. The premise is a philosophy goldmine: what makes Optimus the same being whether robot or truck, do these machines have minds, moral status, or souls, and would real First Contact be with AI explorers rather than biological aliens? As the editors note, probing Transformer nature ends up probing human nature, since they are our own creations.
041 - Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I: Stephen Colbert's The Colbert Report (2005-2014) was a Peabody-winning satire in which he played a blowhard faux-pundit who 'feels the news at us,' coining 'truthiness' — truth by gut feeling — along the way. The character is a philosopher's dream and a philosopher's punching bag. Essays use him to dismantle relativism and the 'right to my opinion,' read his dueling Formidable Opponent segments as real moral deliberation, apply Grice and Russell to nonsense words like 'freem,' and ask whether his Platonic play teaches Americans something Puritanism never let them learn.
042 - Supervillains and Philosophy - Som: Comic-book supervillains — the Joker, Magneto, Lex Luthor, Doctor Doom, Watchmen's Ozymandias — have grown from mustache-twirlers into the most humanized characters in the medium, which is exactly why they deserve philosophy. This volume asks whether anyone can truly will evil, whether tyranny can serve a good cause, why henchmen always betray (Aristotle and Hobbes have answers), and whether Rorschach's unbending Kantianism beats Ozymandias's utilitarian massacre. Essays also test omnipotence with Galactus, personal identity with Venom, and whether Brainiac's disembodied 'pure logic' would actually make him dumber than us.
